Defamatory

dih-FAM-uh-tor-ee · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Defamatory is (of a statement) false and damaging to someone's reputation.

The talent agent threatened legal action after a blog post made defamatory claims that her client had faked his own charity work.

Worked Example

The school board launched an investigation after defamatory flyers wrongly claimed a beloved teacher had been cheating on standardized tests.

The flyers weren't just unkind -- they spread false claims that damaged a real person's reputation, exactly what defamatory describes.

How Defamatory Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

libelous

libelous: containing a written false statement that damages someone's reputation

slanderous

slanderous: containing a spoken false statement that damages someone's reputation

Antonyms

complimentary

complimentary: expressing praise or admiration

flattering

flattering: praising someone in a favorable, appealing way

How Strong Is It? — critical → vicious → defamatory

critical vs. defamatory

critical vs. defamatory: A critical statement is simply negative or fault-finding, which can still be true -- milder and more neutral than defamatory.

vicious vs. defamatory

vicious vs. defamatory: A vicious statement is cruel and deliberately harmful in tone, even more extreme in intent than defamatory.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — de-

prefix — de-: down, injuriously (Latin)

root — fama

root — fama: reputation, report (Latin)

suffix — -tory

suffix — -tory: tending to (as in celebratory) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Defamatory combines de- ('down, injuriously') with Latin fama ('reputation') and -tory ('tending to,' as in celebratory) -- so a defamatory statement is one that tends to drag a reputation down through false, damaging claims.

Word Choice

Defamatory is mostly a legal and journalistic word, describing false statements that damage someone's reputation -- a person or publication can be sued for making defamatory remarks.
